title: Phishing for Information: Spearphishing Link
summary: The link variant moves the victim to attacker-controlled web content where credentials or details are entered. The page is usually a close copy of a real login portal, and the address often contains the genuine brand name plus extra text to look convincing. Attackers also abuse address parsing quirks, such as a user information portion before an at sign or an integer form of a hostname, so a link displays one site and resolves to another. Messages frequently include a tracking pixel, a tiny remote image that confirms the message was opened and records the viewer's address. On the network side the artefacts are proxy and DNS records for a domain the organisation does not use, followed by a successful login that originated at the copied portal rather than the real service.

beginner.definition: This sub-technique puts a link in the message. The link leads to a fake page that copies a real login screen. The victim types a password or personal details into it. It differs from the parent because the message tries to move you to a website. The goal is still to collect information.
beginner.whyItMatters: A copied login page can capture a password that also works on the real system. The attacker then signs in as the victim without any software on the machine. Links can hide where they really go, so the visible address is not proof. A single click can be enough. Blocking lookalike domains early stops a campaign before it reaches people.
howItWorks: The attacker copies a real login page and registers a similar domain name.
They send a message with a link and text that pushes the reader to act fast.
The victim clicks, and the browser loads the fake page over a secure connection.
The victim types a username and password, which the fake page records.
The page may redirect to the genuine site so the victim notices nothing.
A small tracking image in the message confirms that the message was opened.
beginner.example: Think of a market stall that puts up a sign almost identical to the bank across the street. The sign uses the same colours and a similar name. Customers queue at the wrong counter and hand over their details. The real bank sees nothing unusual. A phishing link is that sign, and the queue is your inbox.
takeaways: Check the full address before you type a password anywhere.
Reach important sites by typing the known address or using a saved bookmark.
Watch for newly registered lookalike domains in your network logs.

objectives: Explain how a lookalike login page captures credentials.
Describe the address obfuscation tricks used to disguise a link destination.
Explain the role of tracking images inside a phishing message.
Identify the proxy and DNS records that reveal a phishing click.
Explain how blocking lookalike domains reduces the reach of a campaign.
